title: Respect for suppliants · lines 101–105
subtitle: The god gives the same answer, and Aristodicus starts clearing the birds out of the temple

units.en: That was his question; and the god again gave the same answer, telling them to hand Pactyes over to the Persians.

notes.label: Contrast (μέν ... δέ)
notes.body: Man's question and god's answer are balanced in one sentence, so the reader sees how briefly the god deals with Aristodicus.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Herodotus stresses that nothing has changed, which proves that the first envoys did not misreport the god.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.trans: telling them to hand Pactyes over to the Persians
notes.body: The god repeats the exact words of his first answer (lines 85–86), so the reader sees that he is completely unmoved.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: What follows is planned in advance, which makes Aristodicus' action all the more shocking.

notes.label: Foreshadowing
notes.body: τάδε points forward to something unexplained, so the reader waits to discover his plan.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.trans: going round the temple in a circle
notes.body: He makes a full circuit of the building, so the reader pictures him searching every corner.

notes.label: Imperfect tense
notes.body: The imperfect shows him still at work, nest after nest, which sets up the god's interruption in line 106.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Sparrows are small and harmless, so the reader feels sympathy for the birds he is turning out.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.quote: τοὺς στρουθούς, καὶ ἄλλα ὅσα ... γένη
notes.trans: the sparrows, and all the other kinds
notes.body: The sparrows are paired with every other kind of bird, which shows how thorough he is.

notes.label: Symbolism
notes.body: The birds sheltering in the temple stand for Pactyes sheltering at Cyme, so the reader understands the point Aristodicus is making without being told.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The sacred place where the birds had made their home ends the sentence, which stresses that Aristodicus is violating a sanctuary.

questions: What point is Aristodicus trying to make by removing the birds? Why might he choose to act it out rather than argue it?
How does Herodotus show that this was planned, and not done on impulse?
Before you read on, predict how the god will respond.
